oh yeah, and FUCK gouging satellites! more than once, one of those little fuckers got in my boot, and left a burn trail down the top of my foot.

What's fun about carbon arc is that there are plenty of shapes available for the rods.

I haven't gouged that much with a plasma honestly, maybe I'll order in some tips & give it another go.

IIRC, i used a 100amp TD machine, and had my choice of shallow, shallow-wide, deep, and deep & wide tips. mostly i used it to knock off errant welds for out-of-place parts, so i never really messed with the deep and wide ones, but it worked really well. i was the only one in the shop who even wanted to use the machine, b/c most ppl were accustomed to a torch. house gas was Natural Gas, a real PITA, so the plasma was my first pick. the drawback was i was the one who always got to split beams, and cut out test plates for the whole shop.

The last time I gouged with gas was taking off backplates on test plates in school, it has a more "organic" feel to it. But natural gas ? Ouch ! Poor guys, you make up the price difference on acetylene in saved labor imo.

Being the more proficient one does have it's drawbacks.

we weren't gouging with gas as a regular practice (although i have done that, using a scarfing tip.) that was a different point about everyone else there not wanting to use the plasma to cut up stuff. I saw the plasma as the better cutting tool (making me the go-to cutting guy for long boring cuts,) then discovered it would also gouge. and yes, cutting with natural gas was much suck. i learned how to torch-cut with natural gas, then much later found out how much hotter and faster oxy/acetyline was. IMO, plasma is the way to go for cutting and gouging. it takes a little getting used to without the learner cap on it, but it was the most versatile tool for cutting and gouging altogether, once you get the hang of keeping proper distance from your material.

gouging w/ it was great. no rod in the way, can see your cuts as you go. you can carve as much or as little as you want based on the tip and amps. so if you're rooting around for an imperfection, or the other side of a weld, this was far easier (to see) than carbon arc for me.

I've noticed that most welders usually aren't uppity about changing their ways with new technology... then again sometimes old school ist the best school.
